doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: New York 1948: Tristano and the Miles nonet
title: How he got into Miles Davis's nonet instead of Sonny Stitt
summary: Through Gerry Mulligan and Gil Evans he got the alto chair; he reflects on the balance of his sound and Phil Woods's later version.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Also around that same time you started rehearsing with Miles’ nonet, right?
How did you get involved in that?

Through the Claude Thornhill thing. Miles was friends with Gerry and Gil. [He] came to hear the band. That was basically Gerry and Gil’s band, that’s pretty clear. I think Miles approved of their suggestions, obviously.
Although as you mentioned, they were originally talking about having Sonny Stitt play alto. How did that end up in your favor as opposed to getting Stitt?
I don’t know what happened exactly but I think Gerry talked him out of that in terms of the balance that my sound would add to the ensemble. This was a chamber group.
The music sounds very much like its written with your sound in mind.
Years later when they did it with Phil Woods, I never did hear that record.
[It] was supposed to be different, it had to be different.

Phil played well, I mean he always does, but it’s definitely not the original conception. You’re one of the players it’s really built around: you, Miles, and Mulligan’s baritone sound, the French horn, and Tuba. I think those are the most important components of the sound of that band.
I think Sonny Stitt would have blended in very musically but it would’ve still brought in another weight to his notes, I think.
